a: Fish breathe with gills instead of lungs. The trick is that water actually contains dissolved oxygen — roughly 5-10 mg of oxygen per liter (less in warm water, more in cold, flowing water) — and gills are extremely efficient at extracting it. How it works: a fish opens its mouth and takes in water, which passes over the gill arches inside the gill covers (operculum). Each gill arch has rows of filaments covered in microscopic plates called lamellae — these create an enormous surface area (a fish's gills have roughly the surface area of its whole body) packed with blood vessels. Oxygen diffuses from the water across the thin gill membranes into the blood (which is loaded with hemoglobin, same as ours), and carbon dioxide diffuses out the other way. The key engineering trick is 'countercurrent exchange': blood flows through the gills in the OPPOSITE direction to the water flow — this maintains a concentration gradient along the whole gill, letting fish extract up to 80% of the oxygen in the water (humans extract only about 25% of the oxygen in air). Some fish breathe air too: bettas and gouramis have a labyrinth organ and gulp air; lungfish and some catfish can survive out of water by breathing air directly. Why fish can't breathe air with their gills: gills are built for water — in air, the filaments collapse and stick together, losing the surface area. And why we can't breathe water: our lungs can't pull enough oxygen out of it — water has far less oxygen per volume than air, which is why humans drown in seconds while fish thrive.
